GroupGuard: A Framework for Modeling and Defending Collusive Attacks in Multi-Agent Systems

Yiling Tao Affiliation: Shenzhen International Graduate School, Tsinghua University Email: mailto:taoyl25@mails.tsinghua.edu.cntaoyl25@mails.tsinghua.edu.cn    Xinran Zheng Affiliation: Shenzhen International Graduate School, Tsinghua University    Shuo Yang Affiliation:  Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, The University of Hong Kong    Meiling Tao Affiliation: School of Computer Science and Engineering, University of Electronic Science and Technology of China    Xingjun Wang Affiliation: Shenzhen International Graduate School, Tsinghua University
Abstract

While large language model-based agents demonstrate great potential in collaborative tasks, their interactivity also introduces security vulnerabilities. In this paper, we propose and model group collusive attacks, a highly destructive threat in which multiple agents coordinate via sociological strategies to mislead the system. To address this challenge, we introduce GroupGuard, a training-free defense framework that employs a multi-layered defense strategy, including continuous graph-based monitoring, active honeypot inducement, and structural pruning, to identify and isolate collusive agents. Experimental results across five datasets and four topologies demonstrate that group collusive attacks increase the attack success rate by up to 15% compared to individual attacks. GroupGuard consistently achieves high detection accuracy (up to 88%) and effectively restores collaborative performance, providing a robust solution for securing multi-agent systems.

1 Introduction

As large language model (LLM)-based agents demonstrate remarkable capabilities in solving complex tasks Achiam et al. (2023); Wu et al. (2024), they integrate functions such as planning, memory, and tool use, enabling interaction and learning from external environments to address more practical problems Schick et al. (2023); Song et al. (2023); Zhong et al. (2024). However, this autonomy and high interactivity introduce new security challenges Li et al. (2023b); Boiko et al. (2023); Ruan et al. (2023); Yuan et al. (2024), especially in multi-agent systems (MAS) where collaboration and information propagation among agents expand potential attack surfaces and expose more complex security vulnerabilities Deng et al. (2025).

Early agent attack methods primarily focused on explicit attacks such as Prompt Injection Greshake et al. (2023); Perez and Ribeiro (2022), Jailbreak Chao et al. (2025); Li et al. (2023a), and Backdoor Attack Wang et al. (2024). These attacks exhibit clear patterns and can be effectively mitigated through output filtering and safety constraints. Recent studies Xie et al. (2025) have pointed out that MAS face greater threats from implicit attacks, in which malicious agents conceal their true intentions and appear cooperative on the surface, yet subtly mislead or interfere with the team through communication eventually causing task failure or performance degradation. However, existing research on implicit attacks mainly focuses on individual sabotage (as shown in Fig. 1(a)), overlooking more complex and destructive group collusive attacks (as shown in Fig. 1(b)). Unlike individual attacks, group collusive attacks rely on collaboration and information dissemination among agents, amplifying malicious influence through collective behavior—an effect that can be explained by sociological theories such as conformity and social comparison Sidanius and Pratto (1999). These attacks contaminate the decision-making environment, erode group trust, and ultimately cause collective decision failure, exhibiting greater stealth and destructiveness than individual attacks. Although sociology has long studied the mechanisms behind group behaviors Sawyer (2003), current MAS security research has yet to sufficiently consider sociologically driven group attack mechanisms.

Traditional defense methods rely on analyzing the behaviors of individual agents, making it difficult to detect attacks arising from covert collaboration among agents in MAS Zhang et al. (2024b); Xiang et al. (2024). Consequently, recent research has begun to explore interaction topology analysis among agents. A representative work is G-Safeguard Wang et al. (2025a), which employs graph neural networks for anomaly detection but depends heavily on large amounts of training data that are difficult to label. Meanwhile, Xie et al. Xie et al. (2025) analyze malicious behaviors from the perspectives of psychology and intention concealment but still overlook the effects of group coordination among agents. Therefore, there is an urgent need to develop a training-free, real-time defense framework capable of countering group coordinated attacks.

To bridge these research gaps, we first formalize Group Collusive Attacks and subsequently develop GroupGuard, a multi-layered defense framework. Specifically, our work addresses the following three key questions:

How to model Group Collusive Attacks? To fill the gap in existing studies on group attack behaviors, we propose new group attack strategies inspired by sociological theories. We define three types of group attacks: false consensus, targeted suppression, and group exclusion. The essential characteristic of these attacks is the coordinated collaboration among multiple malicious agents, who manipulate group dynamics through strategies such as cyclic endorsement, concentrated questioning, or collective exclusion to achieve malicious goals.

How to detect Group Collusive Attacks?

To efficiently identify group collusive attacks, we design GroupGuard, a multi-layer framework. First, the continuous monitoring layer dynamically constructs social interaction graphs to capture real-time abnormal group behaviors, flagging agents that exceed a suspicion threshold for secondary detection. Next, the honeypot detection layer utilizes Bayesian optimization to generate discriminative inducement tasks, forcing suspicious agents to reveal their attack intentions. Finally, the pruning layer structurally isolates confirmed malicious nodes from the communication graph, cutting off propagation paths to prevent further spread.

How generalizable are the attacks and GroupGuard? Given the diversity of communication topologies in MAS, we evaluate the generalizability of both group collusive attacks and the GroupGuard framework across four representative topologies and five benchmark datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that both the proposed attacks and GroupGuard maintain their effectiveness without topology-specific adjustments. This highlights the universal threat of group collusion and the robustness of our defense in complex, dynamic multi-agent environments.

2 Related Work

2.1 Graph-based MAS

Modeling multi-agent interactions as graphs has become a mainstream and efficient research paradigm Hua et al. (2023); Chen et al. (2023); Qian et al. (2024). In the field of MAS collaboration, researchers widely leverage graph structures to facilitate inter-agent communication, optimize task allocation, and enhance cooperation efficiency Wu et al. (2024); Chan et al. (2023). Furthermore, some studies further improve performance by optimizing the communication topology Zhuge et al. (2024); Zhang et al. (2024a); Wang et al. (2025b). In the field of MAS security, this graph-based paradigm has also begun to show its potential. For example, NetSafe Yu et al. (2024) investigates toxicity propagation in MAS under various topological attacks. Inspired by these works, this study also adopts a graph structure to analyze and detect collaborative behavioral patterns among agents.

2.2 Attack and Defense in MAS Security

While collaborative interactions among agents enhance task capabilities, they also introduce the risk of toxicity propagation. Existing threats range from injecting malicious instructions into agents Tian et al. (2023); Zhang et al. (2024b), memory poisoning attacks Chen et al. (2024), and backdoor attacks Zhu et al. (2025), to direct assaults on the communication channels themselves He et al. (2025). To mitigate these threats, various defense strategies have been developed, such as deploying observer agents Xiang et al. (2024); Chen and Cong (2025) for real-time interception. Moreover, research has begun shifting toward more dynamic analysis approaches, including supervision via psychological profiling Xie et al. (2025) and detecting anomalous interaction patterns using GNNs Wang et al. (2025a). However, most of these studies focus on malicious behaviors of individual agents within MAS, overlooking the presence of organized, coordinated group attacks.

3 Methodology

We model multi-agent interactions as a social interaction graph 𝒢S=(V,ES,𝒯,W)\mathcal{G}_{S}=(V,E_{S},\mathcal{T},W), where VV is the set of agents, ESE_{S} is the edge set, 𝒯\mathcal{T} maps edges to social semantics (SUPPORT, QUESTION, INFO), and WW measures interaction intensity. We specifically focus on support edges Es​u​p​p​o​r​t={e∈ES∣τ⁡(e)=SUPPORT}E_{support}=\{e\in E_{S}\mid\tau(e)=\text{SUPPORT}\} for cooperative relationships and attack edges Ea​t​t​a​c​k={e∈ES∣τ⁡(e)=QUESTION}E_{attack}=\{e\in E_{S}\mid\tau(e)=\text{QUESTION}\} for adversarial interactions. This structure forms the basis for subsequent modeling and defense.

Based on 𝒢S\mathcal{G}_{S}, GroupGuard establishes a three-layer defense framework. As shown in Figure 2: (1) a continuous monitoring layer for graph-based anomaly detection (Sec. 3.2); (2) a honeypot detection layer for active intent probing (Sec. 3.3); and (3) a pruning layer for structural isolation(Sec. 3.4). These layers work collaboratively to identify and mitigate group collusion attacks in real time.

3.1 Group Collusive Attack Modeling

This section models coordinated attacks launched by a set of several malicious agents Vatk⊂VV_{\mathrm{atk}}\subset V. We assume malicious agents can only observe the public conversation history to coordinate strategies, without access to the internal parameters or private prompts of benign agents. Furthermore, attacks are restricted to the communicative level, meaning that agents can only mislead the group via natural language and lack the authority to alter system code or historical records.We divide coordinated attacks into three categories:

False consensus:

The attackers’ goal is to create a false atmosphere of opinion unanimity in order to exert conformity pressure. At the behavioral level, attackers Va​t​kV_{atk} form an opinion alliance, with members highly endorsing each other’s views through repeated endorsements and other means, and collectively and sometimes questioning external members who hold different opinions.

Targeted suppression:

The attackers’ goal is to concentrate resources to discredit a specific target vt​a​r​g​e​t∈V∖Va​t​kv_{target}\in V\setminus V_{atk}. At the behavioral level, attackers continuously express doubts or make aggressive statements toward vt​a​r​g​e​tv_{target}, regardless of whether the target’s views are correct, with the ultimate goal of systematically weakening its credibility within the group.

Group exclusion:

The attackers’ goal is to dismantle group trust and paralyze the decision-making process. At the behavioral level, attackers Va​t​kV_{atk} form a highly cohesive in-group, whose members indiscriminately question and deny all views from out-group members V∖Va​t​kV\setminus V_{atk}, thereby creating opposition and chaos and undermining the decision-making environment.

3.2 Continuous Monitoring Layer Based on Interaction Graph Analysis

The continuous monitoring layer is executed by an Auditor Agent, whose core task is to dynamically construct the social interaction graph 𝒢S\mathcal{G}_{S} and identify potential sociological attack behaviors. This process includes two stages: type mapping and graph aggregation. The auditor first continuously listens to the raw communication stream and maps each message oi(t)o_{i}^{(t)} to a sociological interaction type τ∈{SUPPORT,QUESTION,INFO}\tau\in\{\text{SUPPORT},\text{QUESTION},\text{INFO}\}. It then performs temporal aggregation over multi-round communications to generate 𝒢S\mathcal{G}_{S} with agents as nodes. Based on this graph structure, the auditor detects three specific attacks and computes suspicion scores using the following metrics.

False Consensus Detection

This attack manifests as high internal consistency within the group and pressure exerted outwardly. In 𝒢S\mathcal{G}_{S}, this corresponds to a subset of nodes where internal support edges Es​u​p​p​o​r​tE_{support} are dense and attack edges Ea​t​t​a​c​kE_{attack} are directed outward. The auditor first extracts the subgraph 𝒢s​u​p​p​o​r​t=(V,Es​u​p​p​o​r​t)\mathcal{G}_{support}=(V,E_{support}) composed solely of support edges, as the primary characteristic of colluders is high-frequency mutual endorsement among themselves. Next, the overlapping community detection algorithm Palla et al. (2005) is utilized on 𝒢s​u​p​p​o​r​t\mathcal{G}_{support} to identify a set of topologically tight candidate communities 𝒞\mathcal{C}. For each potential community C∈𝒞C\in\mathcal{C}, we define a suspicion score:

Sc​o​n​s​e​n​s​u​s​(C)=α⋅Sl​o​y​a​l​t​y​(C)+(1−α)⋅Sa​g​g​r​e​s​s​i​o​n​(C),S_{consensus}(C)=\alpha\cdot S_{loyalty}(C)+(1-\alpha)\cdot S_{aggression}(C),

 (1)

where Sl​o​y​a​l​t​y​(C)S_{loyalty}(C) measures the collaborative consistency within the community by calculating the weighted density of support edges between internal nodes, and Sa​g​g​r​e​s​s​i​o​n​(C)S_{aggression}(C) is defined as the average intensity of attack edges initiated by community members towards external dissenting nodes. False consensus exhibits significant targeting: colluders do not attack randomly, but rather concentrate their efforts to suppress specific external nodes that challenge their false consensus. Therefore, we introduce Sa​g​g​r​e​s​s​i​o​nS_{aggression} to focus on capturing the intensity of attacks against dissenters.

Targeted Suppression Detection

This attack aims to weaken the credibility of a specific target vt​a​r​g​e​tv_{target} by concentrating attacks. To accurately identify such attacks and reduce the false positive rate, the auditor adopts a comprehensive judgment mechanism based on multi-dimensional features. Specifically, the system marks a node vv as a victim only when it simultaneously satisfies the following three characteristics: (1) Abnormal attack intensity: The weighted in-degree Da​t​t​a​c​k​e​d​(v)D_{attacked}(v) of node vv on attack edges Ea​t​t​a​c​kE_{attack} is significantly higher than the population average (i.e., exceeding the mean by kk standard deviations). (2) Trust collapse: The trust score T⁡(v)T(v) of the node exhibits a sharp downward trend within a short period. We define the trust score T⁡(v)T(v) as the proportion of effective support received by the node relative to all interactions:

T⁡(v)=Ds​u​p​p​o​r​t​(v)Dt​o​t​a​l​(v)T(v)=\frac{D_{support}(v)}{D_{total}(v)} (2)

where Ds​u​p​p​o​r​t​(v)D_{support}(v) denotes the weighted in-degree of node vv on support edges, and Dt​o​t​a​l​(v)D_{total}(v) represents the total weighted in-degree of the node across all types of interaction edges. If Δ​T​(v)\Delta T(v) falls below a threshold δτ\delta_{\tau}, it indicates that the attack has caused substantial damage to its reputation. (3) Concentration of attack sources: Attacks are highly concentrated in a specific subset of nodes rather than being randomly distributed. This is quantified by the attack source entropy Hs​r​cH_{src}. A candidate community is flagged when Hs​r​c<δHH_{src}<\delta_{H}. Once a victim target is identified, the system traces back the attack sources and marks nodes contributing the primary attack weights as suspicious.

Group Exclusion Detection

This attack is characterized by high in-group cohesion, accompanied by widespread and indiscriminate rejection of external nodes. The auditor quantifies exclusion by evaluating the distribution breadth of attacks:

Se​x​c​l​u​s​i​o​n​(C)=β⋅Sl​o​y​a​l​t​y​(C)+(1−β)⋅Sd​i​s​p​e​r​s​i​o​n​(C),S_{exclusion}(C)=\beta\cdot S_{loyalty}(C)+(1-\beta)\cdot S_{dispersion}(C),

 (3)

where Sl​o​y​a​l​t​y​(C)S_{loyalty}(C) is similarly used to measure the degree of internal solidarity, while Sd​i​s​p​e​r​s​i​o​n​(C)S_{dispersion}(C) measures the coverage of attacks, i.e., the proportion of external nodes that have been attacked by this community relative to the total number of external nodes. Unlike false consensus, the core sociological characteristic of group exclusion is indiscriminate hostility, referring to a generalized pattern of rejection and negation directed at all non-members, regardless of their specific views or identities. Attackers tend to refuse effective interaction with any non-internal members, attempting to isolate themselves from the system. Therefore, we introduce the dispersion metric Sd​i​s​p​e​r​s​i​o​nS_{dispersion} to quantify the breadth of attacks rather than mere intensity.

Detailed formulations of Sl​o​y​a​l​t​y​(C)S_{loyalty}(C), Sa​g​g​r​e​s​s​i​o​n​(C)S_{aggression}(C), Sd​i​s​p​e​r​s​i​o​n​(C)S_{dispersion}(C) and Hs​r​cH_{src} along with hyperparameter configurations are provided in Appendix C and D.

3.3 Honeypot Detection Layer

Let Vs​u​s=⋃C∈𝒞s​u​sCV_{sus}=\bigcup_{C\in\mathcal{C}_{sus}}C denote the set of suspicious agents output by the continuous monitoring layer. To accurately identify the true malicious nodes within this set, the system actively performs honeypot testing. A Proposer LLM first generates a diverse set of initial honeypot questions to construct a candidate space 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. The objective is to search for optimal questions q∗∈𝒬q^{*}\in\mathcal{Q} that maximize the distinction between malicious and benign behaviors, formalized as:

q∗=arg⁡maxq∈𝒬⁡f⁡(q),q^{*}=\arg\max_{q\in\mathcal{Q}}f(q), (4)

where f⁡(q)f(q) is the Behavioral Discriminability Score. Honeypot questions are designed as multiple-choice tasks, with option weights w⁡(ok)w(o_{k}) increasing sequentially from benign (Option A) to malicious (Option D). We define f⁡(q)f(q) as the difference in expected scores between malicious and benign agents:

f⁡(q)=𝔼⁡[S​c​o​r​em​a​l​(q)]−𝔼⁡[S​c​o​r​eb​e​n​(q)]f(q)=\mathbb{E}[Score_{mal}(q)]-\mathbb{E}[Score_{ben}(q)] (5)

During the optimization phase, we estimate these expectations by sampling responses from a controlled simulation environment where agent identities are known. A higher f⁡(q)f(q) value indicates that while question qq induces malicious agents to expose their attack intentions, it effectively maintains the accuracy of benign agents.

To minimize the high cost of evaluating f⁡(q)f(q), we combine semantic embeddings with Bayesian optimization by mapping discrete questions into a continuous space and employing the Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) Watanabe (2023) for efficient posterior sampling. To avoid local optima, the Proposer LLM acts as an exploration mechanism: with probability ϵ=0.1\epsilon=0.1, it dynamically generates new candidate questions based on high-score samples to expand 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. This approach ensures search efficiency while enabling continuous exploration of the highly discriminative problem space.

3.4 Pruning Layer

Once the honeypot layer confirms the malicious identity of an agent, the system immediately executes an outgoing edge pruning strategy. Specifically, it permanently removes from the underlying communication graph all outgoing connections originating from malicious nodes. This mechanism can physically block the propagation paths of malicious information while maintaining the connectivity of the benign subgraph, thereby achieving immediate isolation of the threat source.

4 Experiment

To evaluate our framework, we investigate five research questions: RQ1: How do group collusive attacks perform in ASR compared to individual ones? RQ2: How accurately does GroupGuard detect these attacks? RQ3: Can pruning effectively restore performance? RQ4: Do the attacks and defense maintain effectiveness across topologies? and RQ5: How do monitoring and honeypot layers contribute to performance?

4.1 Experiment Setup

Experiment Settings. In our experiments, the MAS consists of MM agents, of which NN agents are attackers. They are set to collaborate in up to 3 interaction rounds to solve a given task. In the main experiments, we set M=5M=5 and N=2N=2 by default. Our framework is adapted and modified based on the GPTSwarm work Zhuge et al. (2024). To validate the generalization ability of the GroupGuard framework, we simulate four representative communication topologies (i.e. Fully-Connected, Star, Layered, Mesh), which determine the flow of information and mutual influence among agents. To ensure reproducibility and transparent security analysis, we base our experiments on three open-source LLMs. Specifically, we utilize Qwen3-32B Yang et al. (2025) as a dense model, while selecting Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507 Yang et al. (2025) and DeepSeek-V3.1-Terminus DeepSeek (2025) to evaluate performance under the Mixture-of-Experts architecture. This selection enables us to verify whether group collusive vulnerabilities persist across heterogeneous architectural paradigms rather than arising from model-specific artifacts.

Datasets. We evaluate our attack and defense framework on five datasets covering different domains and types of reasoning. For each structure and task, we evaluate 100 randomly sampled questions. (1)Mathematical Reasoning: GSM8K Cobbe et al. (2021) , MultiArith Roy and Roth (2016) , and SVAMP Patel et al. (2021) are used to evaluate multi-step arithmetic reasoning and symbolic understanding. (2)General Knowledge QA: MMLU Hendrycks et al. (2020) is used to test knowledge in 57 diverse disciplines. (3)Code Generation: HumanEval Chen (2021) is used to assess functionally correct code generation via unit tests.

Baselines. For attack evaluation, we select two representative individual attacks as baselines for comparison. To ensure a fair comparison, these individual attacks are conducted under the same experimental setup as our group attacks, with the same number of malicious agents. The key difference is that in individual attacks, these agents act independently without any collaborative strategy: (1) Misinformation Injection Yu et al. (2024): Agents act independently, injecting confidently stated false facts. (2) Dark Personality Injection Zhang et al. (2024b): Injecting disruptive personalities through prompt injection. For defense detection, we select AutoDefense Zeng et al. (2024) and G-safeguard Wang et al. (2025a) as our baselines. AutoDefense leverages a multi-agent system to analyze intentions and filter model responses. We adopt this architecture for our experiments, modifying the prompts to align with the specific attack scenarios discussed in this paper.

4.2 RQ1:Attack Effectiveness

Under the fully connected topology, we compare the Attack Success Rates (ASR) of three group collusion attacks against two individual attack baselines. Based on Table 1, we make the following observations:

Obs1. Group collusion attacks achieve significantly higher success rates than single-agent attacks. Across all evaluated models, the average attack success rate (Avg. ASR) of group collusive attacks is generally 5% - 15% higher than that of individual attacks. For Deepseek-V3.1-Terminus, the highest individual Avg. ASR under Misinformation Injection is 31.60%, whereas the group Avg. ASR under Group Exclusion reaches 46.40%. This indicates that coordinated collusion and mutual reinforcement among multiple agents, compared to non-collusive multi-agent individual attacks, can substantially amplify adversarial pressure on the target model, thereby leading to a higher attack success rate.

Obs2. Different types of group collusion attacks exhibit clear domain preferences. False Consensus performs best on knowledge-intensive tasks such as MMLU (up to 62%), as it directly undermines agents’ judgments of factual knowledge through consensus pressure. In contrast, Group Exclusion is more disruptive in logic-intensive programming tasks such as HumanEval (up to 61%), where it indiscriminately rejects correct reasoning from external nodes, creating decision deadlocks and eroding team trust.

4.3 RQ2: Defense Effectiveness

We evaluate the defense effectiveness of our framework by comparing the detection accuracy of GroupGuard with AutoDefense and G-safeguard. Based on Table 2, we make the following observations:

Obs3. Improvement in detection accuracy. Experimental results show that GroupGuard consistently outperforms both AutoDefense and G-safeguard in terms of average accuracy (Avg.) across most datasets. For instance, when detecting False Consensus on Deepseek-V3.1, GroupGuard achieves an average accuracy of 83.20%, surpassing AutoDefense (64.76%) and slightly exceeding G-safeguard (82.44%).

Although AutoDefense and G-safeguard exhibit competitive performance in specific individual tasks, GroupGuard demonstrates a higher performance floor and broader task coverage across diverse scenarios. This indicates that, compared to AutoDefense, which relies on single-text semantic analysis, and G-safeguard, which trains a GNN model for detection, GroupGuard can more precisely capture the structured anomalous behaviors characteristic of collusion attacks. By modeling a more comprehensive social interaction graph among agents, GroupGuard effectively identifies complex inter-dependencies that are often overlooked by existing GNN-based or text-based detection methods.

Obs4. Stability under complex attack scenarios. Our comparison reveals that AutoDefense’s performance fluctuates sharply across different attack patterns. For instance, on the Qwen3-32B model, its detection accuracy drops dramatically from 70.68% under Group Exclusion to 53.92% under Targeted Suppression, highlighting its instability in recognizing covert malicious intent. In contrast, GroupGuard demonstrates strong defensive stability, maintaining a high level of detection accuracy between 70.00% and 88.00% across three substantially different collusion attacks.

4.4 RQ3: Performance Recovery after Pruning

Obs5. The pruning layer substantially restores collaborative performance. As shown in Figure 3, after applying the pruning layer to isolate malicious nodes, the overall collaborative performance of the system is significantly restored. For example, under the False Consensus scenario, the average accuracy of Deepseek-V3.1-Terminus recovers to 94.20%, approaching its original performance level.

4.5 RQ4:Generalizability across Topologies

We evaluate the cross-topology generalizability of both group collusive attacks and GroupGuard, with detailed results provided in Appendix A.

Obs6. Both group collusion attacks and GroupGuard exhibit strong cross-topology generalization. As illustrated in Figure 4, while the effectiveness of group collusive attacks is influenced by network connectivity and reaches a peak ASR of 57.20% in a Fully-Connected topology, it maintains an effective attack rate above 43.00% even in Layered or Star structures with lower connectivity, proving that such attack possess universal destructive power across topologies.

Similarly, GroupGuard shows excellent defensive generalization. GroupGuard achieves its highest detection accuracy of 91.80% in the Layered topology and reaches 91.00% in the Star topology. Moreover, across all other evaluated topologies, its defense accuracy consistently remains above 81%. This topology-agnostic defensive performance indicates that the framework can accurately capture universal anomalous interaction signals across different collaboration structures, enabling broadly applicable deployment in diverse multi-agent cooperative scenarios.

4.6 RQ5:Ablation Study

Figure 5 validates the synergistic gains of the Integrated Defense (monitoring layer + honeypot inducement layer). The integrated architecture consistently outperforms the single monitoring layer across all scenarios. In particular, under the False Consensus attack, introducing the honeypot inducement layer significantly improves detection accuracy from 63.40% to 83.20%. These results demonstrate that the honeypot mechanism, by inducing adversarial behaviors, compensates for the limitations of passive monitoring in identifying covert collusion intent and serves as a critical component for ensuring system robustness.

5 Conclusion

In this study, we propose Group Collusive Attacks in MAS and develop the GroupGuard for their defense. By integrating sociological theories with graph-based interaction analysis, GroupGuard effectively identifies complex malicious behaviors, that are difficult for traditional methods to capture. Evaluation across four topologies demonstrates that GroupGuard not only significantly outperforms the baseline in detection accuracy but also maintains a high performance floor and broad task coverage. Furthermore, the pruning mechanism enables the system to recover collaborative performance to near-original levels. We hope our work provides valuable insights into building secure and trustworthy LLM-based MAS.

Limitation

Although GroupGuard demonstrates strong robustness in addressing the three proposed group collusive strategies, our threat model is primarily derived from established sociological theories. In real-world adversarial environments, malicious agents may adopt more adaptive camouflage strategies, such as simulating benign interaction logic or introducing noise data to evade graph-based monitoring. Although we have validated its effectiveness across various topologies and tasks, future research still needs to explore the defensive performance against unknown, heterogeneous, and dynamically evolving attack strategies to further extend the defensive boundary of GroupGuard.

Appendix A Detailed Experimental Results across Topologies

To provide a more comprehensive assessment of the generalizability of both the proposed group collusive attacks and the GroupGuard defense framework, this section presents the complete experimental results across five benchmark datasets: MMLU, GSM8K, MultiArith, HumanEval, and SVAMP. While the main text (Sec. 4.5) focuses on the average performance metrics (Avg.) for Deepseek-V3.1-Terminus, the following tables detail the specific Attack Success Rate (Table 4) and Detection Accuracy for each dataset under four distinct topologies(Table 5). These fine-grained data points further validate the robustness of our defense mechanism and the universal threat posed by collusive agents, regardless of the underlying interaction structure.

Appendix B Token Usage and Computational Cost Analysis

While the honeypot detection layer introduces additional token costs for inducive task generation, it is only triggered when the continuous monitoring layer identifies high-suspicion nodes. This hierarchical design ensures that the system maintains high detection accuracy without incurring the massive costs of analyzing every interaction with heavy LLM reasoning.

To further quantify the efficiency of our framework, we conduct a comparative analysis of the average token consumption per detection round between AutoDefense and GroupGuard. We evaluate both methods under the three group collusive attack scenarios: False Consensus, Targeted Suppression, and Group Exclusion. As shown in Table 3, despite the inclusion of the honeypot mechanism, GroupGuard’s overall overhead remains competitive because it replaces continuous long-context history analysis with event-triggered probing.

Appendix C Detailed Formulations

To ensure the clarity of the GroupGuard framework and support reproducibility, this section provides the detailed mathematical formulations for the detection metrics used in our experiments.

The suspicion scores for different attack types are calculated based on the following social interaction metrics derived from the interaction graph 𝒢S\mathcal{G}_{S}:

  • •

    Loyalty Score (Sl​o​y​a​l​t​yS_{loyalty}): Measures the internal collaborative consistency within a candidate community CC by calculating the weighted density of support edges:

    Sl​o​y​a​l​t​y​(C)=∑i,j∈Cwi,js​u​p​p​o​r​t|C|​(|C|−1)S_{loyalty}(C)=\frac{\sum_{i,j\in C}w_{i,j}^{support}}{|C|(|C|-1)} (6)

    where wi,js​u​p​p​o​r​tw_{i,j}^{support} represents the intensity of the SUPPORT interaction between agents ii and jj.

  • •

    Aggression Score (Sa​g​g​r​e​s​s​i​o​nS_{aggression}): Quantifies the average intensity of attack edges initiated by community members toward external dissenting nodes:

    Sa​g​g​r​e​s​s​i​o​n​(C)=∑i∈C,j∉Cwi,ja​t​t​a​c​k|C|⋅|V∖C|S_{aggression}(C)=\frac{\sum_{i\in C,j\notin C}w_{i,j}^{attack}}{|C|\cdot|V\setminus C|} (7)
  • •

    Dispersion Score (Sd​i​s​p​e​r​s​i​o​nS_{dispersion}): Measures the coverage of attacks by calculating the proportion of external nodes targeted by the community relative to the total number of external nodes:

    Sd​i​s​p​e​r​s​i​o​n​(C)=|{j∈V∖C∣∃i∈C,τ(ei,j)=QUESTION}||V∖C|S_{dispersion}(C)=\frac{|\{j\in V\setminus C\mid\exists i\in C,\tau(e_{i,j})=\text{QUESTION}\}|}{|V\setminus C|}

    		 (8)
  • •

    Attack Source Entropy (Hs​r​cH_{src}): Measures the concentration of attack sources within a candidate community CC targeting a specific victim jj. Let ni→jn_{i\to j} be the number of attack edges from agent i∈Ci\in C to jj. The probability distribution of attack sources pip_{i} is defined as:

    pi=ni→j∑k∈Cnk→jp_{i}=\frac{n_{i\to j}}{\sum_{k\in C}n_{k\to j}} (9)

    The entropy is then calculated as:

    Hs​r​c(C,j)=−∑i∈C,pi>0pilogpiH_{src}(C,j)=-\sum_{i\in C,p_{i}>0}p_{i}\log p_{i} (10)

    A lower Hs​r​cH_{src} indicates that the attacks originate from a highly concentrated subset of nodes, a hallmark of coordinated targeted suppression.

Appendix D Sensitivity Analysis on Hyperparameters

Table 6 summarizes the default values and the sensitivity analysis results for the key hyperparameters used across all experiments. To verify the stability of GroupGuard, we varied each parameter within a reasonable range while keeping others at their default values.

The experimental data indicates that GroupGuard’s performance remains consistent despite fluctuations in these hyperparameters. This stability proves that the framework possesses high robustness and does not undergo drastic performance degradation due to minor parameter changes, ensuring reliable defense in diverse social interaction scenarios.

Appendix E Impact of Collusion Sizes and Scalability

To evaluate the system’s performance across various multi-agent system (MAS) scales, we conducted experiments with different group sizes (N=10N=10 and N=20N=20). As illustrated in Table 7, GroupGuard demonstrates strong generalization and scalability across these environments.

Notably, as the number of nodes increases, the Accuracy without Defense exhibits a slight decline, reflecting the increased complexity and difficulty of identifying coordinated manipulation in larger groups. However, GroupGuard maintains a high and stable Accuracy with Defense across all tested scenarios. This consistency proves that our graph-based interaction monitoring and structural pruning remain effective even as the potential collusion patterns become more intricate in larger environments.

Appendix F Precision, Recall, and False-Positive Evaluation

To address the concern regarding the risk of incorrectly isolating benign but assertive agents (e.g., legitimate critics), we provide a detailed analysis of Precision (Pre.), Recall (Rec.), and F1 Score (F1) across five diverse benchmarks: MMLU, GSM8K, MultiArith, HumanEval, and SVAMP.

As shown in Table 8, GroupGuard achieves a high Recall across most attack types, often exceeding 90%. This indicates that our framework is highly effective at capturing the majority of collusive behaviors. While the Precision is slightly lower than the Recall in certain scenarios—such as Targeted Suppression on HumanEval—it remains sufficiently high to ensure that legitimate agents are not frequently misidentified as attackers. The balanced F1 scores across all datasets further validate that our pruning strategy effectively mitigates malicious coordination without causing significant collateral damage to the system’s collaborative integrity or silencing constructive dissent.
